PAPER: Artificial Intelligence Review (2026) 59:4 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10462-025-11411-7 Designing a robust extreme gradient boosting model with SHAP-based interpretation for predicting carbonation depth in recycled aggregate concrete Meysam Alizamir1,2 · Aliakbar Gholampour3 · Sungwon Kim4 · Salim Heddam5 · Jaehwan Kim6 Received: 19 May 2025 / Accepted: 23 September 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract The degradation of concrete structures is significantly influenced by carbonation, where atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO ) penetrates the concrete matrix. Measuring how far 2 carbonation penetrates into concrete plays a vital role in maintaining structural integrity and construction safety standards. Precisely forecasting the extent of carbonation pen- etration in recycled aggregate concrete (RAC) remains fundamental for understanding long-term performance and durability. This research is the first to introduce an innovative approach that leverages eight machine learning algorithms to estimate carbonation pen- etration depth. The selected techniques include NGBoost, GBRT, AdaBoost, CatBoost, XGBoost, LightGBM, HistGBRT, and MLR. Moreover, to evaluate model accuracy, four key performance indicators were employed. Additionally, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was incorporated for enhanced model interpretability. Furthermore, the inves- tigation examined six distinct input parameter configurations during training and test- ing to thoroughly assess model performance. Among the evaluated algorithms, XGBoost delivered the highest accuracy, with an RMSE of 1.389 mm, MAE of 1.005 mm, and R of 0.984. CatBoost followed closely, with RMSE of 1.772 mm, MAE of 1.344 mm, and R of 0.976. Then, the LightGBM ranked third in effectiveness, exhibiting an RMSE of 1.797 mm, MAE of 1.296 mm, and R of 0.975. These results demonstrate the reliability and interpretability of advanced machine learning models for carbonation depth estima- tion in RAC. The developed models offer practical tools for engineers seeking to evaluate how carbonation penetration affects structural integrity. These findings establish a strong foundation for understanding and predicting carbonation-related deterioration in concrete infrastructure. The depletion of natural aggregates and the environmental burden of construction waste have led to the adoption of recycled aggregate concrete (RAC) as a viable alternative to conventional concrete (Hasheminezhad et al. 2024). The RAC, produced by incorporat- ing recycled aggregates obtained from demolished concrete structures, provides substantial advantages by reducing carbon emissions, preserving natural resources, and minimizing landfill waste. (Xing et al. 2022). However, despite these advantages, the RAC exhibits distinct mechanical and durability properties compared to traditional concrete, necessitating a thorough understanding of its long-term performance (Wu et al. 2024). One of the major durability concerns in concrete structures is carbonation, a process wherein atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO ) penetrates the concrete matrix and reacts with 2 calcium hydroxide (Ca(OH) ), forming calcium carbonate (CaCO ) (Tang et al. 2015; Mal- 2 3 ami et al. 2021; Al Salaheen et al. 2023). This reaction reduces the alkalinity of concrete, ultimately leading to the depassivation of embedded steel reinforcement and an increased risk of steel corrosion (Mi et al. 2023). In RAC, the carbonation depth (CD) is generally higher than in traditional concrete, primarily due to the increased porosity of recycled aggre- gates and the weaker interfacial transition zone (ITZ), which accelerates CO₂ diffusion and alters the microstructural integrity of the material (Del Bosque et al. 2020). Experimental studies have explored various factors influencing the carbonation behavior of RAC, including aggregate replacement ratio, aggregate size, curing methods, and cement composition. For example, Otsuki et al. (2003) studied how to improve the carbonation resistance of RAC. They showed that the RAC with double mixing method developed a higher resistance compared to that of the single mixing method. Silva et al. (2015) studied the effect of different factors, such as the aggregate replacement level, size and origin, on the carbonation of RAC. The concrete with 100% recycled aggregate developed two times 1 3 Designing a robust extreme gradient boosting model with SHAP-based… Page 3 of 39 4 the CD compared to the natural aggregate concrete. They also reported that the concrete with finer recycled aggregates exhibited a higher CD, and the strength of the parent concrete had little to no effect on the CD of the RAC considering that the aggregates obtained had similar water absorption (Silva et al. 2015). Tang et al. (2018) showed that the carbonation age of RAC increased with carbonation age. They also reported that the long-time carbon- ation resistance of the RAC could be improved by small compression loading. Leemann and Loser (2019) studied the effect of clinker content of the cement on the carbonation resistance of RAC. They showed that the carbonation coefficient of the concrete decreased with decreasing the clinker content. Mi et al. (2025) showed that the carbonation increased the inhomogeneity of RAC through dividing the RAC into irregular carbonation and non- carbonation zones. While these studies have provided valuable insights into the mechanisms governing carbonation in RAC, their findings highlight the complexity and variability of carbonation behavior, necessitating reliable predictive models to accurately estimate CD under different conditions. Given the widespread use of the RAC in structural applications, accurately predicting its CD is crucial to ensuring the longevity and reliability of RAC- based constructions. Traditional experimental approaches to assess the CD of RAC have been labor-intensive, time-consuming, and sensitive to variations in environmental conditions (Golafshani et al. 2024). As an alternative, data-driven modeling techniques have emerged as powerful tools for predicting the CD with enhanced efficiency and accuracy (Malami et al. 2021). Artificial intelligence approaches excel at processing datasets with various inputs and outputs, uncov- ering connections between different factors (Alizamir et al. 2020a, 2025a; Khan and Abbas 2023; Lai et al. 2024; Zhang et al. 2024; Abbes et al. 2024; Elmousalami et al. 2025). For example, these techniques have been successfully applied to a wide range of modeling prob- lems across various fields, such as dew point temperature (Alizamir et al. 2018) estimation, wind energy forecasting (Elmousalami et al. 2025), estimation of the compressive strength of copper mine tailings concrete (Alyami et al. 2024), groundwater fluctuation prediction (Alizamir et al. 2020b), estimation of the compressive and tensile strength of basalt fiber reinforced concrete (Ullah et al. 2025), compressive strength forecasting (Khan and Abbas 2023), daily solar radiation prediction (Alizamir et al. 2023a), prediction the compressive strength of cement-based mortar materials (Alyami et al. 2025), and displacement analysis of concrete-filled steel tubular columns (Lai et al. 2024). The framework’s architecture enables concurrent processing of datasets without compromising predictive accuracy (Ke et al. 2017; Zhang et al. 2019; Kakkar et al. 2024). Data scientists frequently turn to LightGBM for its distinctive combination of swift processing, reliable performance, and modest resource requirements, particularly when tackling expansive datasets with numerous features (Hancock and Khosh- goftaar 2021). Unlike traditional methods that build trees level by level, this optimized approach employs depth-restricted leaf expansion (Zhu et al. 2022). Among the top-performing variants of CatBoost1, AdaBoost1, XGBoost1, LightGBM1, NGBoost1, HistGBRT1, GBRT1, and MLR1, XGBoost1 showed the highest accuracy based on the NSE. Specifically, it improved CD prediction performance by 2.07% over CatBoost1, 25.75% over AdaBoost1, 2.28% over LightGBM1, 12.82% over NGBoost1, 10.65% over HistGBRT1, 2.28% over GBRT1, and 91.52% over MLR1. Based on MAE, XGBoost1 also outperformed the other models, with improvements of 33.73% over CatBoost1, 247.46% over AdaBoost1, 28.96% over LightGBM1, 143.88% over NGBoost1, 83.78% over HistGBRT1, 34.93% over GBRT1, and 461.49% over MLR1. These results confirm that XGBoost1 offers the most reliable and accurate predictions for CD among the evaluated models. In addition, recognizing different feature combinations, results showed that the first sce- nario yielded the most accurate predictions, while the sixth scenario performed the worst among ensemble boosting models. For the MLR model, the fifth scenario produced the least accurate results. Due to differences in model architecture, parameter configurations, and hyperparameter settings, the predictive performance varied significantly across ensemble boosting and lin- ear regression approaches. Overfitting and underfitting issues during training could be miti- gated by using high-quality datasets with a wide range of values (Kim and Kim 2008; Gu et al. 2016). Additionally, applying K-fold cross-validation (Fushiki 2011) helps improve model generalization and reduce bias. Several studies have explored CD prediction using machine learning. For example, Huo et al. (2023) developed single and ensemble models (inverse variance and artificial neu- ral networks) and found that ensemble methods outperformed individual models. Wang et al. (2024b) applied eight machine learning models to recycled concrete and reported that automated approaches provided better predictions than conventional equations. Their SHAP analysis identified water-to-cement ratio and carbonation time as key features. Tran et al. (2023) used four single and four hybrid models for concrete with fly ash and found XGBoost to be the most accurate. SHAP analysis also revealed exposure time as the most influential variable. The current study has presented a novel application of ensemble boost- ing and linear regression models combined with SHAP analysis for CD prediction, offering new insights beyond previous research. One limitation of this study was the relatively small dataset, which might affect the generalizability of the results. Future research should expand the dataset and incorporate 1 3 4 Page 32 of 39 M. SHAP analysis of the current study identified ET as the most influential factor affecting CD across all models. This has direct implications for service life estimation and durability design. Longer exposure to CO -rich environments accelerates carbonation and increases 2 the risk of steel corrosion. Engineers can use ET-based predictions to anticipate corrosion onset and schedule timely maintenance. ET can also inform mix design, curing methods, and protective measures, especially for RAC, which is more porous and vulnerable to carbonation. The SHAP-based feature importance analysis also provides actionable guidance for opti- mizing mix designs. High SHAP scores for cement content and recycled aggregate sug- gest that adjusting these parameters can reduce porosity and improve durability. Similar to Alyami et al. (2025), who used SHAP to guide mix design for compressive strength, this study supports data-driven strategies for RAC. For example, reducing water content while maintaining workability and selecting low-absorption recycled aggregates can help mitigate carbonation. The proposed XGBoost-SHAP model offers practical value for real-world construction. Accurate CD prediction enables engineers to tailor mix designs to environmental condi- tions, reduce maintenance costs, and improve durability. Model-guided use of recycled aggregates promotes sustainability by lowering carbon emissions and conserving resources. This approach also streamlines material selection and testing, enhancing both environmen- tal and economic efficiency in concrete infrastructure. 7 Limitations and research directions for future The limitation of this study can be explained as the approach of few ensemble boosting (CatBoost, AdaBoost, XGBoost, LightGBM, NGBoost, HistGBRT, GBRT) and linear regression (MLR) for predicting CD utilizing the small samples. Therefore, this study can- not guarantee generalized success in predicting CD in concrete using the models discussed. Therefore, it is recommended to expand the dataset to better capture variations under dif- ferent conditions. Additionally, the insufficient variety in experimental approaches can be compensated by sustained research efforts incorporating combined ensemble enhance- ment algorithms, bio-inspired optimization strategies, and comprehensive data preparation frameworks to establish superior forecasting results with exceptional reliability metrics. Another limitation of the present work that may be addressed in future studies is that this research focuses exclusively on comparing boosting-based ensemble models for predicting CD. Other widely used machine learning models such as SVR, GPR, ANN, or RF were not considered for performance comparison. 8 Conclusion Carbon dioxide (CO ) infiltration is a major degradation mechanism affecting the structural 2 integrity of reinforced concrete. As atmospheric CO penetrates the concrete matrix, it grad- 2 ually reduces the material’s alkalinity, lowering the pH and creating conditions conducive 1 3 Designing a robust extreme gradient boosting model with SHAP-based… Page 33 of 39 4 to steel reinforcement corrosion. The extent of this chemical transformation, quantified as carbonation depth (CD), is a critical indicator of potential structural compromise. Accurate prediction of CD is essential for assessing durability, preventing corrosion, and extending the service life of concrete infrastructure. In this study, eight machine learning models, including NGBoost, GBRT, AdaBoost, CatBoost, XGBoost, LightGBM, HistGBRT, and MLR, were trained and validated using six different input scenarios to predict CD of recy- cled aggregate concrete (RAC). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was integrated to enhance model interpretability. Key findings include: ● Machine learning models significantly outperformed traditional data fitting approaches in predicting CD across all performance metrics. ● The initial input feature set consistently yielded the most accurate predictions, high- lighting the importance of feature selection. ● Exposure time (ET) emerged as the most influential parameter on CD, followed by ce- ment content (C), recycled aggregate (RA), and fine aggregate (FA). ● XGBoost achieved the highest accuracy, with an RMSE of 1.389 mm, compared to 7.353 mm for MLR. CatBoost and LightGBM followed closely with RMSE values of 1.772 mm and 1.797 mm, respectively. The XGBoost-SHAP framework demonstrated strong predictive capability and interpret- ability, making it a valuable tool for durability assessment and mix design optimization in RAC. Future research should focus on expanding datasets, applying advanced prepro- cessing techniques such as wavelet transforms, and exploring hybrid modeling approaches to further enhance prediction accuracy. This data-driven approach offers practical benefits for construction engineering, including reduced maintenance costs, improved structural performance, and more efficient material utilization. By supporting sustainable design and minimizing environmental impact, the proposed model contributes to the advancement of resilient and eco-friendly concrete infrastructure. JSON: Name: xgboost_shap_carbonation_rac Title: Interpretable extreme gradient boosting with SHAP for predicting carbonation depth in recycled aggregate concrete Short Hypothesis: Training an XGBoost model with the described material and exposure input features causes a statistically significant reduction in RMSE for carbonation depth prediction in recycled aggregate concrete compared to multiple linear regression and other common boosting and tree-based baselines under held-out validation. Related Work: Prior approaches to predicting carbonation depth in recycled aggregate concrete have applied conventional statistical models (multiple linear regression) and a range of machine learning techniques including artificial neural networks, support vector regression, random forests, gradient-boosted trees, and individual implementations of XGBoost and LightGBM. Metaheuristic optimization has been used to tune boosting models in some studies. Interpretability efforts have largely been limited or qualitative; a few recent works employed Shapley-value methods to rank features but lacked systematic cross-model comparisons and ablation over input sets. Reported limitations include small or heterogeneous datasets, inconsistent preprocessing and validation protocols, limited exploration of modern ensemble variants (CatBoost, NGBoost, HistGBRT), scarce probabilistic uncertainty quantification, potential overfitting from aggressive hyperparameter tuning, and insufficient analysis of feature-correlation effects on attribution methods. Abstract: This project addresses accurate and interpretable prediction of carbonation depth in recycled aggregate concrete (RAC) using extreme gradient boosting combined with SHAP-based explanations. We propose a modeling pipeline that (1) compiles an experimental RAC carbonation dataset, (2) trains an XGBoost regression model with systematic hyperparameter optimization, (3) compares predictive performance against multiple baselines (linear regression, Random Forest, GBRT, LightGBM, CatBoost, NGBoost, HistGBRT, AdaBoost), and (4) applies SHAP to generate global and local explanations and to quantify feature importance stability across input subsets. The main contribution is an empirically validated, interpretable XGBoost-SHAP framework that (a) demonstrates statistically significant improvement in point-prediction accuracy and (b) provides ranked, instance-level attributions for exposure time, cementitious and aggregate variables. Expected outcomes include a reproducible evaluation protocol, quantified gains in RMSE/MAE and correlation metrics versus baselines, and an analysis of limitations in attribution caused by feature correlation and dataset heterogeneity, enabling more informed durability assessments for RAC. Experiments: Datasets: assemble a consolidated dataset of experimentally measured carbonation depth (CD) in recycled aggregate concrete from peer-reviewed sources; target N≈475 complete records including features: cement (C), fly ash (FI), water (W), natural coarse aggregate (CA), recycled coarse aggregate (RA), recycled aggregate water absorption (RWA), fine aggregate (FA), and exposure time (ET). Create six predefined feature sets identical to the paper (model1..model6). Preprocessing: impute missing values with median per-study where necessary, standardize numeric features (z-score), and log-transform ET if skewed. Train/test split: stratified random split 70% train / 30% test; additionally perform 10-fold cross-validation within training for hyperparameter selection. Baselines: multiple linear regression (MLR), Random Forest (RF), GBRT, AdaBoost, CatBoost, LightGBM, HistGBRT, NGBoost, and a feedforward ANN with one hidden layer. Primary model: XGBoost regressor. Hyperparameter search: grid or randomized search over learning_rate [0.01,0.05,0.1,0.2], n_estimators [100,300,500], max_depth [3,5,8,10], subsample [0.5,0.7,1.0], colsample_bytree [0.5,0.8,1.0], regularization lambda [0,1,5]; use 10-fold CV to select parameters by minimizing mean CV RMSE. Evaluation metrics: RMSE, MAE, Pearson R, Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE); report mean and 95% confidence intervals on test set via bootstrap (1000 resamples). Statistical tests: paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test on per-fold RMSE between XGBoost and each baseline (alpha=0.05). Ablation studies: (A) Compare performance across the six feature sets to quantify input importance; (B) Holdout study removing ET to quantify dependence on exposure time; (C) Compare XGBoost deterministic predictions to NGBoost probabilistic predictions—evaluate NGBoost negative log-likelihood and calibration (reliability diagrams, sharpness). Explainability analyses: compute SHAP global feature ranking and per-instance force plots for 100 random test samples; quantify attribution stability via Kendall tau between SHAP rankings across 10 bootstrap resamples of training data. Dataset-shift checks: compute Kolmogorov–Smirnov and Jensen–Shannon divergence per feature between train/test. Reporting: provide parity plots, residual histograms, Taylor diagram of standardized error, and tabulated metric comparisons for all models. Risk Factors and Limitations: Limited dataset size and heterogeneity may constrain generalization to unseen concrete mixes, exposure regimes, or measurement protocols; publication-derived data can include inconsistent measurement methods and unknown biases. Collinear features (e.g., cement and water-to-binder proxies) reduce reliability of SHAP attributions and can produce unstable feature rankings. Hyperparameter tuning risk: extensive search may overfit validation folds, yielding overoptimistic test performance if data leakage occurs. NGBoost or other probabilistic models may produce miscalibrated predictive intervals under heavy-tailed or multimodal residuals. Computational cost: grid searches across many ensemble models are time-consuming and may require substantial compute. Evaluation bias: choice of train/test split, bootstrap strategy, or stratification criteria can affect statistical test outcomes. The model trained on compiled experimental data may not generalize to field-cured structures, different CO2 concentrations, or new recycled aggregate sources without additional calibration.
